newsitem.title: FRANCE: Main events in France's Juppe government.
newsitem.headline: Main events in France's Juppe government.

text.p: Following is a chronology of main events since French President Jacques Chirac, after his election in May 1995, appointed Alain Juppe prime minister:
* May 18, 1995 - Juppe takes office saying he wants his government to be judged "on our ability to stimulate in France a deep and durable movement to create jobs".

Launches plan to create 700,000 jobs, increase minimum wage, raise pensions and create new benefits for elderly and children, accompanied by two-point increase in value added tax to 20.6 percent, payroll charge cuts and accelerated privatisation plan.
* August 25, 1995 - Juppe forces free-marketeering Finance Minister Alain Madelin to resign after he assails "privileges" of civil servants.

* October 26, 1995 - Under pressure from financial markets and European Union partners, Chirac abandons quick job creation and tax cut pledges and say his "priority of priorities" is to cut deficits to enable France to qualify for a single European currency.
* November 7, 1995 - Chirac reshuffles the cabinet, leaving Juppe as prime minister but firing half of the women ministers, nicknamed the "Jupettes", appointed six months earlier.

* November 15, 1995 - Juppe announces sweeping reform of the welfare state to streamline public health care, retirement and family benefits and end chronic social security deficits, with a new tax to pay off accumulated debts of the system.
Proposals include making civil servants work longer for a full pension. Plan coincides with proposed reform of SNCF state railways that would end train drivers' right to retire at 50.
New welfare levy takes total increase in tax burden to 120 billion francs ($21 billion) in first 15 months of new government.
Plan draws immediate criticism from trade unions and some health professionals and becomes deeply unpopular with public.
* November-December 1995 - Juppe's welfare and rail reform plans trigger 24-day strike by public transport workers, backed by other public sector workers, that cripples the country.
Juppe drops plan to make civil servants work longer, withdraws rail reform but maintains health care spending limits and management reforms.

* May 1995-April 1997 - Juppe government sells off aluminium giant Pechiney and insurance company AGF but stumbles in trying to privatise defence and electronics firm Thomson, causing diplomatic spat with South Korea when independent privatisation commission refuses to approve sale of Thomson MultiMedia unit to Daewoo. Lagardere Groupe and Alcatel Alsthom tender new bids for Thomson, which government puts on hold until after election.

Plan to sell minority stake in France Telecom provokes opposition from employees and the left. Originally set for May 1997, sale is postponed until after election. Socialists and Communists say they will halt it if elected. Other privatisations on hold include planemaker Aerospatiale.

* September 5, 1996 - Juppe, shown by one poll to be the most unpopular French premier since 1958, announces five-year plan to cut income tax by 75 billion francs with 25 billion in 1997 alone. Increase in savings levy to help fund debt-ridden welfare system reduces net tax cut to 18 billion francs. With increases in local authority taxes, few voters feel better-off.
* November 1996 - Truck drivers blockade French roads for 12 days to win right to retire at 55 and improvements in working conditions. Government presses employers into yielding.

* March-April 1997 - Junior hospital doctors strike against plans to control health costs by fining doctors if their region overshoots spending limits. Government agrees to make fines more selective and defer implementation for newly qualified doctors. Strikers return to work but maintain opposition to plan.
* 1997 - In sporadic labour unrest, airline pilots, train conductors, bank employees and civil servants protest against attempts to withdraw "acquired rights" or change their working conditions.

* April 21, 1997 - Chirac dissolves National Assembly and calls two-round parliamentary election. Says France needs a "new elan" to forge closer European integration and approach a single European currency from a position of strength. ($ = 5.712 French Francs)
